prompt.context: Your client is Procter & Gamble, which owns Tampax and Always, leading menstrual product brands in the US. With the rise in sustainability-focused products, P&G's in-house R&D team has developed a hypoallergenic and eco-friendly high-grade silicone material for use in upcoming product launches. They are interested in using the material to make menstrual cups to add to their line of consumer care products.
prompt.question: Should P&G sell the silicone menstrual cups?

clarifying_info.q: What is P&G's success criterion for this launch?
clarifying_info.a: P&G will manufacture and sell the product if at least 10% of customers willing to purchase menstrual cups are willing to pay for it, and the inherent cannibalization does not negatively impact sales.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the current competitors in the menstrual cup market?
clarifying_info.a: Stand-alone brands such as Diva Cup, Softcup, Blossom, Saalt, and Lena.
The cup is environmentally friendly with an average 5-year lifespan before recycling.

clarifying_info.q: What are the R&D investment costs?
What discount rate should we use?
clarifying_info.a: The compound discount rate for a 5-year period is 10%.

clarifying_info.q: Does P&G own any other menstrual brands?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, P&G owns Tampax (tampons) and Always (pads).

exhibits.title: Survey: Willingness to Switch to Menstrual Cup
exhibits.shows: A pie or bar chart showing results of a survey sent to US women aged 18-50 on their willingness to switch from current menstrual products to a menstrual cup. Survey response rate is 5%.
exhibits.data: Categories include: Yes (would switch), No (would not switch), and Undecided/Neither. 40% of respondents are undecided.

exhibits.title: Current P&G Menstrual Care Product Sales Data
exhibits.shows: A table showing average price, units per package, price per unit, and annual frequency of purchase for P&G's existing menstrual care products.
exhibits.data: Tampons: $6.99 avg price, 28 units, $0.25/unit, 10x/year; Pads: $6.99 avg price, 46 units, $0.15/unit, 2x/year; Liners: $5.99 avg price, 100 units, $0.06/unit, 1x/year

exhibits.title: Estimated Complementary Product Sales Data
exhibits.shows: A table showing average price, units per package, price per unit, and annual frequency of purchase for estimated new complementary products that would be sold alongside the menstrual cup.
exhibits.data: Single-use Discs: $14.99 avg price, 12 units, $1.25/unit, 2x/year; Wash: $6.99 avg price, 1 unit, $6.99/unit, 4x/year; Wipes: $6.75 avg price, 10 units, $0.68/unit, 4x/year

exhibits.title: Survey: Willingness to Pay for Menstrual Cup by Price Tier
exhibits.shows: A table or chart showing survey results of how many respondents fall into each willingness-to-pay price category (Very Likely, Likely, Neither Likely nor Unlikely, Unlikely, Very Unlikely) broken out by price tier. Survey response rate is 5%, total survey respondents: 1,620.
exhibits.data: Total survey respondents: 1,620; survey response rate: 5%; respondents segmented by price tier and likelihood to purchase.

framework: Pricing and Volume: Market size, consumer willingness to pay, competitor prices, cannibalization of existing P&G product sales
Marketing Factors: Sustainability angle, price comparison to alternatives, long-term cost savings for customers, target segments, portability
Competition: New entrants, market saturation, standalone cup brands (Diva Cup, Saalt, etc.)
Financial Feasibility: R&D cost recovery ($12M), cannibalization impact, net revenue from complementary products
Risks: Product cannibalization of Tampax/Always, manufacturing costs, lower-than-expected adoption

questions.prompt: Question 1: Calculate the US market size for the menstrual cup product.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use a top-down approach. Key steps: start with US population, filter to females, apply even age distribution to isolate menstruating-age cohort (10-50), apply willingness-to-use rate, then multiply by comparable product price and market capture rate.

math.setup: Top-down market sizing: US population → female → menstruating age → WTP → price × capture
steps: Even age distribution 0-80, divided into 8 decade bands: 165M / 8 = 20.625M per decade
math.answer: Market size: $330M addressable; Year 1 revenue: $33M (aggressive) to $16.5M (conservative)

questions.prompt: Question 2: Based on Exhibit A (survey results), what adjustments would you make to your market size?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read the survey chart and note that 40% of respondents are undecided. They should recognize that P&G believes it can convert a quarter (25%) of that undecided 40%, bringing effective willingness to use from 10% to 20%. They should then recalculate the market size with 20% WTP.

math.setup: Adjust WTP from 10% to 20% (original 10% + 25% of undecided 40% = 10% + 10% = 20%)
math.answer: Adjusted market size: $660M addressable; Year 1 revenue: $66M (aggressive) to $33M (conservative)

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Part 1): Using Exhibit B, calculate the annual sales per customer for P&G's existing menstrual care products that would be cannibalized.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply average price × annual frequency for each product, then sum to get total annual spend per customer.

math.setup: Annual spend per product = Average Price × Annual Frequency of Purchase
math.answer: Annual sales per customer: ~$90; 5-year cannibalized PV: $675M

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Part 2): Using Exhibit C, calculate the estimated annual sales from complementary products that the menstrual cup would generate.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the same approach to complementary products (discs, wash, wipes) and compute the 5-year PV of complementary revenue.

math.setup: Annual spend per complementary product = Average Price × Annual Frequency of Purchase
math.answer: Annual complementary sales per customer: ~$85; 5-year complementary PV: $637.5M

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Part 3): Calculate the breakeven unit price for the menstrual cup to offset cannibalization.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the formula: Breakeven Price = (Cannibalized Revenue + R&D Costs - Complementary Revenue) / Captured User Market. The answer should be approximately $25-30 per cup.

math.setup: Breakeven Unit Price = (Cannibalized Revenue + R&D Costs - Estimated Complementary Revenue) / Captured User Market

questions.prompt: Question 4: Using Exhibit D and the breakeven price of ~$30, does P&G meet the launch threshold of at least 10% of interested customers willing to pay?
questions.guidance: Candidate should add all respondents at prices of $21+ across the Likely, Very Likely, and a quarter of Neither Likely nor Unlikely categories. Compare total to 10% of 1,620 respondents (= 162K threshold).

math.setup: Sum respondents willing to pay at $21+ tier; compare to threshold of 10% of total respondents
steps: Neither Likely nor Unlikely at $21+: (260 + 156 + 104) = 520; × 25% conversion = 130K
math.answer: 298K willing buyers exceeds the 162K threshold; P&G should launch the product.

brainstorming.prompt: P&G has noticed consumers' increased interest in sustainability. What suggestions would you have for the marketing team to promote the menstrual cup? How can P&G lean into this consumer interest in their other menstrual products?

categories.name: Pro-Cup Marketing (4Ps)
ideas: Product: Emphasize ease of use and new hypoallergenic silicone material
Pricing: Price according to customer WTP and breakeven calculations (~$30)
Place: Distribute through pharmacies and DTC (direct-to-consumer) channels
Promotion: Highlight ease of use, sustainability factors, lifetime cost savings vs. tampons/pads, influencer marketing options

categories.name: Non-Cup Menstrual Products (4Ps)
ideas: Product: Transition to fully biodegradable materials, reduce packaging, provide transparency on ingredients, offer organic product variants
Pricing: Maintain same quality at familiar price points
Place: Continue selling through pharmacies, online retailers, and grocery stores
Promotion: Launch sustainability-focused ad campaigns based on new eco-friendly product upgrades

recommendation: P&G should proceed with launching the silicone menstrual cup. The breakeven unit price of ~$30 is achievable, 298K willing buyers exceeds the 10% threshold (162K), and complementary product revenue partially offsets cannibalization of existing products.
P&G should price the menstrual cup at approximately $30 per unit to offset cannibalization and recover R&D costs within the 5-year product lifecycle.
risks: Excessive product cannibalization of Tampax and Always product lines if adoption exceeds projections
Incorrect estimated revenue and purchasing frequency assumptions in the model
Lower-than-expected market capture or consumer adoption rates
Potentially more profitable applications for the new silicone material in other product categories
next_steps: Develop a comprehensive marketing plan leveraging sustainability messaging; contact current retailers for promotions and shelf placement
Consider expanding product sales to additional international markets
Explore 1:1 donation programs to developing markets as part of the sustainability and brand positioning strategy
